terms.definition: Insurance firm that sold environmental policies worth $100 million each to Velsicol and Fruit of the Loom in 1998.
Adjacent and neighboring properties — a term used in St. Louis for a nine-block area of homes where soils were contaminated with DDT.
Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, a CDC-based Superfund program focused on health assessments at contaminated sites.
A non-Hodgkin lymphoma cluster detected in Breckenridge, Michigan, several miles downwind east of St. Louis.
Radioactive waste facility operated by Velsicol along Bush Creek between St. Louis and Breckenridge.
Superfund site across the river from the old Velsicol plant where wastes were burned; also called the Golf Course site or Velsicol Burn Pit site.
Community Advisory Group — a designation under Superfund regulations. The Pine River Task Force functions as one.
Biologist and author of Silent Spring, who identified the problems caused by Velsicol products; became a symbol of the push for chemical regulation.
Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act — the official name of Superfund, passed by Congress in 1980.
Purchased Velsicol after acquiring Michigan Chemical; later became Northwest Industries and then Fruit of the Loom.
Veterinarian in McBain, Michigan who conducted early PBB exposure identification work on local farms.
A legal settlement in which guilt is not admitted but corrective action is undertaken.
University of Michigan physician who conducted early PBB research.
A pesticide perfected during World War II, produced by Michigan Chemical after 1944; featured prominently in Rachel Carson's work.
Abbreviation for Dense Nonaqueous Phase Liquid.
DNAPL — a syrupy substance composed of contaminants.
Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy, formerly MDEQ or DEQ.
Acronym for environmental justice.
Superfund procedure for highly contaminated sites; conducted in 1999 to remove the worst sediment from the Pine River.

The fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people regardless of race, color, national origin, or income, with respect to the development, implementation, and enforcement of environmental laws.
A policy and behavioral problem that exposes minority communities to disproportionate contamination and less rigorous government enforcement.
President Clinton's 1994 directive requiring federal environmental agencies to prioritize environmental justice in policy implementation.
Fruit of the Loom owner from 1984 to the late 1990s who sold Velsicol to its managers.
Farmers' organization that operated a cooperative feed supply business in Battle Creek where PBB was accidentally mixed with feed.
Flame retardant manufactured by Michigan Chemical, composed of PBB; mistakenly shipped to Farm Bureau in 1973.
Underwear company acquired by Northwest Industries; later sold Velsicol but retained ownership of the St. Louis plant site.
Former solid waste landfill south of St. Louis, Michigan, on Jackson Road, where Velsicol dumped contaminated wastes.
Alternative name for the Velsicol Burn Pit Superfund site west of the Pine River.
Once a highly polluted tributary of the Pine River; cleaned under a Supplemental Environmental Project.
Bi-national agency created in 1909 by Canada and the United States under the Boundary Waters Treaty.
Located in Alma upstream from Michigan Chemical; acquired by Total Refining in 1970.
Core component of Michigan Chemical's animal feed supplement, Nutrimaster.
Operated on the south side of what became Michigan Chemical's St. Louis plant; later part of Great Lakes Chemical.
Michigan Department of Community Health, now called the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.
Michigan Department of Environmental Quality, now called EGLE.
Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.
Founded in 1935 in St. Louis, Michigan; later became part of Velsicol Chemical.
Michigan Department of Public Health, former name of MDHHS and MDCH.
Operated a refinery in Alma, Michigan, upriver from Michigan Chemical.
Under the Superfund program, a list of more than 1,000 of the worst contaminated sites in the country.
National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, part of the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
See National Priorities List.
Former name of Chicago and North Western Railway after acquiring Velsicol and Michigan Chemical in 1965.
Animal feed supplement produced by Michigan Chemical, primarily composed of magnesium oxide.
Subparts of a Superfund site with similar problems resolvable through similar methods; the Velsicol site has several.
See Operable Unit.
Auto parts manufacturer in Alma (formerly Lobdell-Emery) that dumped hexavalent chromium into the Pine River.
Abbreviation for polybrominated biphenyls, a core component of fire retardants.
The 1973 mix-up by Michigan Chemical involving PBB fire retardants and animal feed supplement.
Group of PBB-exposed individuals followed since the 1970s for health consequences; currently overseen by Emory University.
Para-chlorobenzenesulfonic acid, a DDT production byproduct found in St. Louis's old water system.
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances — over 9,000 human-made chemical types often called "forever chemicals" due to their environmental persistence.
Tracks serving the Michigan Chemical/Velsicol plant; originally part of the Pere Marquette Railroad, later Chesapeake and Ohio, then CSX Corporation.
A ROD — the Superfund term for EPA's announcement of a cleanup plan, including the formal public comment process.
Founder of Velsicol Chemical; also patented the window envelope.
See Record of Decision.
Physician and occupational health pioneer at Mt. Sinai School of Medicine who led early PBB studies.
Velsicol's worst contamination locations, including the St. Louis plant site and Breckenridge dump; not assumed by Velsicol after its split from Fruit of the Loom.
Rachel Carson's 1962 bestseller criticizing chemicals patented by Velsicol; Velsicol attempted to prevent its publication.
A civil engineering technique used to build reinforced concrete walls in areas of soft earth close to open water, designed to prevent contaminated groundwater migration from the Velsicol site.
Multi-polluter dump site on State Road and Jackson Road south of St. Louis; state-regulated, not a Superfund site.
EPA-administered program for cleaning up America's most contaminated sites; St. Louis has three designated sites.
A SEP — a legal process converting pollution fines into community projects.
Technical Assistance Grant, allowing communities to obtain independent review of EPA cleanup decisions.
Book ghost-written for Congressman Jamie Whitten, funded by Velsicol and Shell Chemical to attack Rachel Carson's work.
France's largest oil company; acquired Leonard Refining in Alma in 1970.

terms.term: United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration
terms.definition: UNRRA — a World War II-era refugee agency that purchased substantial DDT quantities from Michigan Chemical.
Describes a polluter able to ignore consequences because wind and water carry pollution away from their own location.
Founded in 1931 in Chicago by Joe Regenstein; acquired Michigan Chemical in 1965.
Michigan State University ornithologist who conducted pioneering research on DDT's impact on birds; targeted by chemical industry criticism.
